en: The Sūtra on the Son of a Good Family, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhi Fadu.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. There...
At that time, the householder Sujāta was gravely ill and near death;
he instructed his son, saying, "After I have passed away, you must perform the six-directional prostrations.

Subsequently, Sujāta died. His son then respectfully escorted and made offerings for him; once the funeral rites were completed, he would rise early each morning, bathe, put on new clothes, go to the water's edge, and pay homage to the six directions, saying:
"I pay respectful homage to you with solemnity because you were born in the eastern direction; you, in turn, shall pay me respect.
He repeated these words in the same manner as he circumambulated the south, west, north, above, and below.

At that time, as the Buddha was about to enter the city at dawn, having dressed and taken up his alms bowl, he saw the householder Sunakṣatra’s son performing obeisances in this manner from six directions upon the water.
The World-Honored One then followed him and asked:
"Householder’s son!
What is your name?"

I have recently heard that you will surely rise early to bathe, put on new clothes, go to the water's edge, and pay obeisance to the six directions while saying, "With reverence and solemnity, I pay homage to all quarters," and then bathe once more.
"What is the teacher’s instruction for that which is worthy of respect,
son of good family?
The son of good family replied:
"My father, when he was on the verge of death, first gave this instruction; it is for this reason that I follow it, not because I heard it from a teacher.
The World-Honored One replied, "Son of a householder!..."
"What my father spoke of was not these six directions.

Rather, if one sits amidst the desires of the six faces and possesses defiled and evil conduct on four sides, yet is unable to repent, then upon the death of the body, the spirit shall be reborn within the hells of the evil realms."
A person should recognize that there are four things that constitute weariness. What are these four?
First, a fondness for killing living beings; second, a fondness for theft; third, lewd and depraved conduct; and fourth, a delight in false speech.
The Buddha expressed this meaning in verse:
"Killing living beings, stealing, Deceiving through false speech,
and Lusting after the wives of others— These are not praised by the wise."
"Furthermore, householder’s son!
There are four things that lead one to the evil realms.
What are these four?
"First is desire, second is anger, third is delusion, and fourth is fear.
To explain its meaning, he recited these verses:
"With desire, anger, delusion, and fear, One does not receive the True Dharma."
Therefore, one who is named as being in a lower position is like the moon in its dark phase,
waning and diminishing; yet one who is free from desire, anger, delusion, and fear, and who receives and upholds the True Dharma,
is therefore named as being in a higher position, like the moon in its bright phase, waxing and reaching fullness.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
There are six afflictions that consume wealth and lead one into evil destinies; you should recognize them.
What are the six? "

First is indulgence in wine and dissipation; second is entering the rooms of others at improper times; third is dissipation through gambling; fourth is a great fondness for music and performance; fifth is evil companionship; and sixth is indolence.
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
“Drinking alcohol, entering another’s chamber, gambling, and delighting in performers and singers,
evil companions and indolence— these are not praised by the noble sages.”
"Now, there are six transformations of wine that one ought to know.
What are these six? They are:
the depletion of wealth, the provocation of illness, the incitement of strife, the increase of anger, the loss of reputation, and the impairment of wisdom."
"Once this evil exists, one's undertakings will fail; wealth not yet acquired will not be obtained, and that which has already been acquired will vanish, until former stores are completely exhausted.
One should know that there are six transformations of sexual depravity."

What are the six? They are: not protecting oneself; not protecting one's wife and children; not protecting one's family members; giving rise to evil through doubt; providing an opportunity for enemies; and being surrounded by manifold sufferings.
Once this evil exists, one’s undertakings will fail; wealth not yet acquired will not be obtained, and that which has already been acquired will vanish until former savings are completely exhausted.
One should know that there are six stages to gambling.
What are the six?

Victory gives rise to enmity; defeat causes inner distress. Friends grieve for one, while enemies rejoice. There is the misfortune and anxiety of imprisonment, and the multitude of people harbor doubts.
Once this evil exists, one's undertakings will fail; wealth not yet acquired will not be obtained, and that which has already been acquired will vanish until former stores are completely exhausted.
One should know that there are six transformations of such fondness for pleasure.
What are the six? They are:
being intent on dancing, intent on singing, intent on stringed instruments, intent on rhythmic clapping, intent on drums, and intent on others.
When one possesses these evils, one's undertakings are ruined; wealth not yet acquired is not obtained, and that which has already been acquired perishes, until former stores are entirely exhausted.
"One should know that there are six transformations of an evil friend.

What are the six? Habitual indulgence in intoxication and delusion; habitual indulgence in confusion and disorder; habitual indulgence in license and self-indulgence; habitual indulgence in taverns; habitual association with petty people; and habitual indulgence in vulgar speech."
When such evil exists, one’s undertakings are abandoned; wealth not yet acquired is not obtained, and that which has already been acquired perishes, until former stores are utterly exhausted.
One should know that there are six transformations of indolence.
What are the six? Not working when full; not working when hungry; not working when cold; not working when hot; not working at dawn; and not working at dusk.
When one possesses such evils, one’s undertakings are abandoned; wealth not yet acquired is not obtained, and that which has already been acquired is dissipated until former stores are exhausted.
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"Delighting in fine forms, music, and song, resting by day and following such things at night—
through evil friends and indolence, a man suffers great loss."
Addicted to gambling and wine, their minds are set on women;
they distance themselves from the wise and draw near to the foolish, their decline like the waning moon.
In their conduct, they are self-conceited and arrogant, disparaging and belittling the path of the śramaṇas.
One who holds wrong views yet practices stinginess is called a man of arrogant and dissolute character.
Now, alcohol obstructs the use of wealth; though its profit is small, it causes great thirst when drunk.
It brings about illness, water-borne debt, and the commission of disturbances that endanger one’s life and invite disease.
Some form friendships through wine; some commit crimes because of it.
If it leads to the accomplishment of great benefit, such instances may yet be tolerated.
Others observe the precepts by day, yet act with villainy on the path at night.
Always frequenting wine-shops— be careful never to associate with such as these.
From winter to summer, like grass that does not value itself,
if one exerts diligence in worldly affairs, one's benefit will thereby be diminished.
If one can endure cold and heat, Like grass that holds no regard for itself,
And diligently cultivates one's endeavors, Then there will be peace and benefit.
Associating with the lowly leads to gradual decline, While practicing with the superior never causes harm.
Advancing in goodness is transcendent and honored; by means of goodness, one will surely obtain goodness.
Great goodness leads to meeting with goodness; if one can sincerely practice both forms of goodness, it is what one's kinsmen esteem—one upholds the precepts to extinguish evil.
Therefore, one should practice accordingly; having already practiced, one practices further.
As for being foremost among kinsmen, it is like a sovereign presiding over the multitude.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
There are four types of pseudo-friends who are not true friends; one should recognize them. What are the four?
First, those who take another's property; second, those who speak with flattery; third, those who show affection only in one's presence; and fourth, those who provide false teachings.
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"To take as friends those who possess alien things, Whose words are beautiful only to flatter the ear,
Who speak with sycophancy and affection in person— Such false teachers bring one peril."
Because these do not possess the marks of a true friend, the wise do not befriend them;
having recognized them, one should distance oneself from them, just as one leaves a treacherous path.
One who befriends those of different character should know this through four matters.
"What are the four? They are:
coveting another's property; giving little while hoping for much; practicing out of fear; and practicing for the sake of profit.
To express its meaning in verse:
"Taking that which belongs to another, giving little while desiring much, fearing the habituation to gain and the habituation to profit—the greedy person’s circle of friends is thus.
This is not the mark of a friend; it is one with whom the wise do not associate."
"Once recognized, one should distance oneself from them, just as one emerges from a treacherous path.
One should know a sycophantic friend by four things.
What are these four?"
"He proclaims the private affairs of others while concealing his own; he feigns virtue to their faces but spreads slander behind their backs.
Its meaning is praised in verse:
"He delights in proclaiming the private affairs of others, / While having private matters of his own that he conceals."
To flatter one's face while praising their goodness, yet to discuss their faults behind their back—this is the mark of a non-friend. Such a person is not a friend to the wise;
once recognized, one should distance oneself from them, just as one would leave a treacherous path.
"One should know a friend who feigns affection by four matters.
What are these four?
Speaking of another's past faults, secretly seeking their future transgressions, not bestowing wealth upon them, and wishing for them to encounter misfortune."
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"To do what should not be done, To find no benefit in creating false speech,
To give without regarding it as a treasure, And to pray for oneself when others are in distress."
Because these are not the marks of a friend, the wise do not befriend them;
having recognized them, one should distance oneself from them, just as one leaves a treacherous path.
A friend of false teachings should be known by four matters.
"What are the four? They are:
encouraging and transforming others through the act of killing; encouraging and transforming others through theft, sexual misconduct, and deceitful fraud.
To express this meaning in verse:
"Taking life and stealing, Deceitful false speech,
and lusting after another’s wife— One who encourages others in these ways is no true friend;
A wise person does not befriend such a one."
"Once recognized, one should distance oneself from them, just as one leaves a treacherous path.
Furthermore, son of a householder, there are four kinds of friends who are benevolent and desire to benefit others; these you should recognize and know."
"What are the four?
First, sharing in suffering and joy; second, supporting one another for mutual benefit; third, providing for their original livelihoods; and fourth, acting with benevolent compassion.
To express this meaning in verse:
Sharing both safety and peril with others, Guiding them through wholesome benefits,
Acting as a benefactor who can sustain people, And compassionately leading them onto the right path—
Such is the likeness of a friend, That which the wise study and recite.
"One should associate with such a person; they will surely cause one to increase in goodness and not do evil.
A friend who shares in both suffering and joy should be known by four things.
What are these four?"
"Give that which you yourself treasure; give for the benefit of your wife and children; give all that belongs to the household; speak with loyalty and practice patience.
To praise this meaning, it is said:
"Rather than benefiting oneself, Even if one possesses wealth and profit, one should give it away."
To provide for one's family’s benefit, and to speak with loyalty and patience—such is the likeness of a friend, whom the wise cultivate and cherish.
One should associate with such as these; they will surely bring increase and never do evil.
"A friend who is beneficial and supportive should be known by four qualities.
What are these four?
They do not disclose one's private matters; they do not conceal their own private matters; they speak kind words to one's face; and they work to quell slander against one."
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"By not proclaiming another's private faults and not concealing one's own,
speaking of what is good when meeting and conversing, one shall, upon returning, have calmed all slander."
Such is the likeness of a friend whom the wise cultivate and associate with;
one should engage in such company, for it will surely bring benefit and not lead to evil.
One should recognize a friend from former karma by four things.
"What are the four?
To employ them through the industry of profit; to employ them through the industry of strength; to admonish them against self-indulgence; and to nourish them with goodness.
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"Supporting one with wealth and profit, assisting in security through strength,
tempering one's excesses and indulgences, and nurturing one's virtuous aspirations—
such is the likeness of a friend, whom the wise cultivate and hold dear."
One should engage in this practice; one will surely increase in goodness and not do evil.
"A friend who is compassionate and pities one should be known by four things.
What are the four?"
"By teaching and exhorting them to stand firm, one brings their faith to completion, their precepts to completion, their learning to completion, and their generosity to completion.
To praise this meaning, it is said:
"The path of faith, precepts, learning, and generosity— One should constantly use these to exhort and transform others."
"One who is such as this is the likeness of a friend, whom the wise cultivate and associate with;
one should engage in their company, for it will surely bring benefit and not lead to evil.
Furthermore, son of a householder!..."
Now, facing east is like a son seeing his parents.
Therefore, a son ought to rectify his reverence, nourishment, and comfort for his parents through five matters.

What are the five? They are: mindfulness in reflecting on the affairs of one's household; attending solely to the discharge of debts and obligations; attending solely to the understanding and observance of precepts; attending solely to the rendering of offerings; and attending solely to the joy of one's parents.
Furthermore, parents ought to love and cherish their children through five matters.
What are these five? They are:

establishing a foundation for their livelihood; planning profitable undertakings with them; arranging a marriage for them; teaching them the Way and the precepts of the scriptures; and entrusting them with all that they possess.

This constitutes the first two divisions of the eastern quarter: that which one desires is the attainment of the laws established by the ancient sages—being filial as a son and being compassionate and loving as a parent—so that the aspirations of gentlemen increase and wholesome dharmas do not decline.
"Now, one who faces south is like a disciple seeing his teacher.
Therefore, a disciple should rectify his reverence, nourishment, and comfort toward his teacher through five matters."
What are these five?
One must be diligent in hearing the teachings, diligent in loving learning, diligent in attending to affairs, free from transgressions in conduct, and must provide for and honor one's teacher.
Furthermore, the teacher should compassionately instruct the disciple through five matters.
What are these five?

To cause them to study through their own learning, to perfect their skills through instruction, to make them diligent in study, to guide them with the path of goodness, and to introduce them to virtuous friends.

These constitute the two divisions of the southern quarter. As for what is desired: one obtains the laws established by the ancient sages; as a disciple, one is humble, and the teacher instructs with benevolence; thus the aspirations of the gentleman increase, and wholesome dharmas do not decline.
"Facing west is like a husband looking upon his wife.
Therefore, the husband should rectify his respect for her, provide for her, and ensure her comfort through these five matters."
What are the five?

She should serve him with a correct mind and respect; she should harbor no resentment in her heart and have no other affections; she should provide him with food and clothing at the proper times, and provide him with precious ornaments at the proper times.
Furthermore, a wife should serve her husband through fourteen matters.

What are the fourteen? They are: performing good deeds; accomplishing what is good; receiving instructions with careful attention; rising at dawn; retiring at night; ensuring that all tasks are learned; keeping the door closed to wait for the gentleman; when the gentleman returns, inquiring after his well-being; being harmonious in tone and demeanor; being compliant in speech; setting out the mats and seats properly; purifying food and drink; being mindful of giving; and making offerings to one’s husband.

This constitutes the second division of the West: that which is desired is the attainment of the laws established by ancient sages, the propriety of husband and wife, the advancement of the gentleman, and the non-decline of wholesome dharmas.
"Now, one who faces north is like a friend meeting his companion.
Therefore, a friend should rectify his companions through five matters: rectifying their reverence, rectifying their nourishment, and rectifying their peace."
What are these five?

One should serve them with a correct mind and respect; one should harbor no resentment in one's heart, harbor no ulterior motives, share food and flavors with them from time to time, and never cease showing them profound kindness.
Furthermore, a friend should also attract their companion through five matters.

What are the five? To have those who fear [retribution] return to me; to frequently reprove those who are negligent; to conceal private matters for them; to cause their offerings to increase and improve over time; and to speak with loyalty and patience.

This constitutes the second division of the northern quarter: that which one desires—the acquisition of the laws established by ancient sages, the cultivation of friendship with companions, the increase of a gentleman's reputation, and the non-decline of wholesome qualities.
"Now, as for those below him, they are like the elder son’s slaves, retainers, and attendants.
Therefore, the elder son ought to rectify, nourish, and settle these slaves, retainers, and attendants through five matters."

What are the five? Employing them according to their strength; providing them with food and clothing at the proper times; sharing choice flavors with them from time to time; instructing them in the fasts from time to time;
and providing medical care when they are ill. Furthermore, the slaves, servants, and attendants should provide for the eldest son with ten matters.

What are the ten? They are: performing deeds well; accomplishing what is well done; receiving instructions with careful attention; sleeping at night; rising early; learning diligently in all matters; working with diligent effort; not being indolent despite poverty; not becoming despondent in times of want; and when going out, being praised, saying, "The eldest son of my family is intelligent and wise."

This constitutes the second division of the lower direction: that which is desired is the attainment of the laws established by ancient sages and the propriety of the eldest son’s administration of affairs; thus the aspirations of the noble man increase, and wholesome dharmas do not decline.
"Now, 'being on high' is like a person living at home who encounters śramaṇas and brahmins.
Therefore, when they come to one's home, one should properly honor, properly nourish, and properly settle them with five matters."

What are the five? Opening the gate to wait for them; going out to meet them and inquiring after their well-being; providing seats and mats for them; protecting the treasury of the sutras and the Dharma; and offering pure food.
By these means one makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins.
Furthermore, śramaṇas and brahmins should respond to the families that provide alms with five matters.

What are these five? They are: instructing them so as to perfect their right faith; instructing them so as to perfect their ethical conduct; instructing them so as to perfect their extensive learning; instructing them so as to perfect their generosity; and instructing them so as to perfect their wisdom.

This constitutes the two parts of the higher direction: that which one desires—the attainment of the laws established by ancient sages, the propriety of householders, recluses, and brahmins, the increase of a man’s aspirations, and the non-decline of wholesome qualities.
The meaning of this is expressed in verse:
"The father and mother face east; The teacher’s seat should face south;
The son and wife face west; The position for friends faces north."
Servants and attendants should be placed below, while śramaṇas and brahmins should be placed above;
this is how one should pay respect, and it is likewise appropriate for those living as householders.
When an ordinary person possesses wealth, they should keep in mind using it to benefit others.
Sharing wealth and profit with others, the one who practices giving ascends to heaven.
Sharing the gains one obtains with others, one finds peace wherever one goes.
For those who embrace the world through righteousness, this is the root of proximate happiness.
To gather people through kindness is like a mother toward her child;
by skillfully protecting and sustaining the world, one’s blessings will repeatedly accrue.
Having attained a place among the great assemblies, one is able to provide benefit, profit, and peace.
Fulfilling the trust and precepts of an adult, one must surely attain renown.
With a mind that is never indolent, one abandons the practice of stinginess;
one gathers people through acts of friendship and bestows gifts of food and drink.
Coming and going, yet departing once more—this is what is called being without deficiency.
One who is able to cultivate carefulness of the person is a worthy one within the household.
Those who dwell in the accumulation of treasures and goods should promote benevolence and righteousness.
First, study is most excellent; next is the cultivation of one's livelihood.
If one seeks to acquire wealth, it should always be divided into four parts:
one part for food and clothing, and two parts for capital to seek profit.
Set aside one part as a reserve; it may be used to save you in times of distress.
To support farming and commerce, one raises cattle; the livestock business has four branches.
Next, the fifth is to maintain and adorn the household; the sixth is to marry.
In this way, wealth is accumulated, increasing day by day. Indeed,
as riches gather night and day like a stream flowing into the sea,
one should manage one's estate gradually, just as a bee produces honey.
Though possessing wealth, one has no one to share it with; likewise, one has no one to share the frontier regions with.
Through stinginess and evil karma, one has strength but no friends.
One should learn to apply oneself to matters when they arise; if not, do not let yourself be hindered.
Observe those who employ such practice: their clarity and joy are like a blazing fire.
Among their kinsmen and relatives, they enjoy a twofold excellence;
sitting at ease with the assembly of kin, they are like Śakra dwelling in his celestial palace.

Thereupon, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, the son of Śuka prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and circumambulated him three times; with a joyful heart, he took refuge and received the precepts from the Buddha.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Son of a Good Family (Suvīraputra-sūtra)
